# Practical Exercise: Blocking in 2^k^ experiments 

This exercise is useful for the following courses:

- 161.222;
- 228.371;
- and general revision on experimental design topics.

## Aims of this practical exercise


In this exercise you will:

- fit the model for a randomised complete block experiment, using multiple treatment factors this time;
- investigate main effects and interaction plots; and,
- find the treatment means and their standard errors.


## Before you undertake this exercise...

Let's load the packages we will need.


``` {r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor) 
library(ggfortify)
library(FrF2)
library(emmeans)
```


## The Paper gloss dataset (revisited)

The dataset is from a paper plant which produces large rolls of paper. The paper is run through a machine called a 'super calendar' to provide a gloss to the paper. The response variable is the gloss of the paper. 

When we used this dataset before, the treatment variables speed (S), pressure (P), and temperature (T) were combined together into a single treatment factor called Treatment. For example, Treatment 1 was low-speed, low-pressure and low-temperature, while treatment 8 was high-speed, high-pressure, high temperature. Let's use the three factors now.

### Data Preparation


Recall that there were 3 replicate measurements taken of the paper's gloss on each day, For each treatment combination. The data was presented in a wide format. The data manipulations done previously for this data are condensed below.


``` {r}
Paper <-read.csv("https://R-Resources.massey.ac.nz/reworked/SandersEtAl2002.csv") |>
    mutate(across(c(Day:Treatment), factor)) |> 
    pivot_longer(cols=c(Rep1,Rep2,Rep3),values_to = "Gloss",names_to = "Replicate") |> 
    arrange(Day,Treatment,Replicate) |>
    glimpse()
```

## The model

Fit the linear model suitable for this randomised complete block design, using the three two-level factors and their interactions.


You should also check out the residual analysis for this model.

```{r}
Paper.lm1 <- lm(Gloss ~ Day + S *P*I, data = Paper)
anova(Paper.lm1)
```
There are significant main effects, but no significant interaction effects. 

Linear model assumptions appear to be met. 

```{r}
plot(Paper.lm1)
```


## Suitable graphs

Generate the main effects and interaction plots for this data. Make sure you have the right packages loaded.


```{r}
MEPlot(Paper.lm1)
```

```{r}
IAPlot(Paper.lm1)
```
The main effects are noteworthy, but interactions effects are not. 


#### Calculating marginal means

We need to think differently when we calculate the mean effect of each treatment. Do we need to use interactions? Can we ignore other factors?

We will use the `emmeans()` package again.

For example, if we could be sure that speed has no interaction with other factors, we would use:


``` {r}
emmeans(Paper.lm1, "S")
plot(emmeans(Paper.lm1, "S"))
```

```{r}
Paper.lm2 <- lm(Gloss ~ Day + S + P + I, data = Paper)
anova(Paper.lm2)
```
```{r}
plot(emmeans(Paper.lm1, "S"))
plot(emmeans(Paper.lm1, "P"))
plot(emmeans(Paper.lm1, "I"))
```


N.B. This command will throw warnings if the model used has interactions which have an impact on the factor being considered. Before you implement the command, fit the model that includes only the significant effects.

```{r}
plot(emmeans(Paper.lm1, c("S", "P", "I")))
```
